content:
Kavu styles internal links with bracketed [[wikilink]] markers — a convention borrowed from Roam, Obsidian, and the wider tools-for-thought tradition. The brackets are added by the theme; you write ordinary Markdown links.
Recommended form #[Note Maturity Stages](/notes/note-maturity-stages/) This produces: Note Maturity Stages — note the brackets that Kavu adds around the rendered link.
How the resolver works #The theme’s render-link.html partial inspects each link:
External links (anything starting with http, https, mailto:, or #) render as plain anchor tags, no brackets, opening in a new tab. Internal links starting with /notes/ are matched against page URLs. This is the recommended form. Anything else falls back to matching the link text against page titles. So [Welcome to Kavu](welcome) works if a page titled “Welcome to Kavu” exists, but breaks the moment you rename the link text. Use absolute /notes/slug/ paths and you’ll never have a broken internal link.
Backlinks #Every note page automatically lists its backlinks at the bottom. You don’t maintain them by hand — the theme scans page content and inverts the link graph. See the bottom of What Is a Digital Garden for an example.
Related # Welcome to Kavu What Is a Digital Garden
summary: Internal links between notes render with [[bracket]] markers. Use absolute /notes/slug/ paths so the resolver finds the target every time.
title: How Wikilinks Work

content:
Kavu uses a status field in note frontmatter to mark how mature each note is. The three values map to colours in the network graph and badges on each note page:
Status Meaning Colour seeding 🌱 A stub or rough thought. Maybe a single sentence. Amber growing 🌿 A developed draft. Linked to a few neighbours. Still rough at the edges. Blue evergreen 🌳 Polished, well-linked, represents a stable understanding you’d point a friend at. Green The system has two halves. The first half is a low bar for creating notes — write a seedling the moment a thought arrives, even if it’s one line. The second half is a high bar for promoting notes — evergreen means you’d actively recommend it. Most notes will sit at growing forever, and that’s fine.
The practical effect is that you get to publish in public without performing finality. A reader can see at a glance whether they’re reading a stub or a stable claim.
Related # Welcome to Kavu What Is a Digital Garden Seedling Example
summary: Kavu uses three labels — seeding, growing, evergreen — to mark how mature a note is. Lower the bar for publishing; raise it for promotion.
title: Note Maturity Stages

content:
This site is an example garden built with Kavu, a Hugo theme for digital gardens and personal knowledge bases. The notes you see are short, generic samples meant to demonstrate the theme — feel free to delete them all and start your own garden in their place.
A few things to try right now:
Open the What Is a Digital Garden note and follow the links inside it. Notice the bracketed [[wikilink]] rendering — that’s How Wikilinks Work. Scroll back to the homepage and look at the Network graph. Each dot is a note, coloured by maturity. Hover and click around; press / to search. Check the colour-coded dots in the index. Green is evergreen, blue is growing, amber is a seedling. The system is explained in Note Maturity Stages. If you’re starting fresh, the Seedling Example shows what a half-formed thought looks like — Kavu is built around the idea that publishing rough notes is fine.
Related # What Is a Digital Garden Note Maturity Stages How Wikilinks Work
summary: What this theme does, what to look at, and where to go next.
title: Welcome to Kavu

content:
A digital garden is a personal website organised around ideas and the links between them, rather than around chronology. A blog is a stream — newest at the top, posts finished and forgotten. A garden is a network — notes are added, revised, cross-linked, and allowed to mature in public.
Three things tend to be true of digital gardens:
Notes are small and atomic. One idea per page. Titles are claims or concepts, not headlines. Notes link densely to each other. A reader can wander between related ideas without going through a navigation menu. Notes have visible maturity. Half-formed thoughts are allowed and labelled as such — see Note Maturity Stages. The metaphor is older than the web. A garden is cultivated, but never finished. It is a place you walk through, not a feed you scroll. Kavu (കാവ്, Malayalam for sacred grove) leans into the metaphor.
A real one in the wild #The Kavu theme was built for, and is used by, stultus.in/notes — the digital garden of Hrishikesh Bhaskaran. Browsing it is the easiest way to see what the theme looks like with a few hundred densely cross-linked notes covering software, philosophy, and storytelling.
Related # Welcome to Kavu Note Maturity Stages How Wikilinks Work
summary: A digital garden is a personal site organised by ideas and links rather than by dates. Notes grow over time.
title: What Is a Digital Garden
